## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to reason about 128-bit bit patterns and implement branchless validation using bitwise operations. Prefix masks are fundamental in networking for CIDR blocks and subnet calculations; validating them efficiently is a practical skill.

## Key Concepts
- **Prefix masks**: A contiguous sequence of 1-bits followed by 0-bits (e.g., 11110000...). Valid values include all zeros (0) and all ones (128).
- **128-bit arithmetic**: Must handle carry propagation between low and high 64-bit halves.
- **Bit-reversal trick**: Converts the MSB-first prefix property into an LSB-first property that can be validated with a simple carry-propagation check.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests precise bit-mmask construction under edge-case shifts; no loops/branches is a common constraint in low-level systems.

## Key Concepts
- Bit masks and ranges
- Safe shifts with variable width (1..32)
- No branching; single expression mask composition

## Code Example
```javascript
uint32_t clearRange32(uint32_t x, unsigned a, unsigned b) {
  unsigned w = b - a + 1; // width of range
  uint32_t ones = (~0u) >> (32 - w); // w ones in LSBs
  uint32_t mask = ~(ones << a); // zeros in [a,b], ones elsewhere
  return x & mask;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to generalize to 64-bit with the same constraints?
- What if inputs are signed; does behavior change in C/C++?

Tests low-level bit manipulation skills without branches, common in performance-critical code. It demonstrates proper masking, shifting, and word size preservation.

## Why This Is Asked
Tracks cross-word parity using SWAR folding without branches.

- Multi-word parity with bitwise folding
- SWAR technique to reduce 64-bit to 1 bit
- No loops or branches across 256 bits

unsigned parity256(uint64_t a,uint64_t b,uint64_t c,uint64_t d){

## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?

## Why This Is Asked
This checks understanding of 128-bit bit rotations using only shifts and masks, with a branch-free formula.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise shifts and modulo wrap-around
- 128-bit arithmetic and safe shifts
- Branch-free expression design

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateRight128(uint128 x, uint64_t r){
  r &= 127; // 0..127
  return (x >> r) | (x << ((128 - r) % 128));
}
```
